passage:
I sit two desks from Hafsa in a shared office, so I see the Monday routine. The dashboard tab stays shut. Hafsa opens a design tool, refills the water bottle, answers messages. Once I joked, "Have you looked at the numbers?" and got a bright "Later!" I felt uneasy but didn't push.
This month a letter from the bank arrived. Hafsa read it standing up, sat down slowly, and finally opened the dashboard. I glimpsed a line sloping down for four months. Hafsa said only, "Okay," and cancelled the planned hire. I can't say whether it was fear or plain exhaustion I was watching.
By evening there was one cheaper plan left on the notepad.
— Nandini

qa.q: How long had the line on the dashboard been sloping down?
qa.a: It had been sloping down for four months.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been feeling each Monday while keeping the dashboard tab shut?
qa.a: Probably dread about the numbers, though Nandini cannot be sure: the closed tab and the bright "Later!" suggest Hafsa was steering away from something painful.

qa.q: What could Hafsa have done differently on those Mondays?
qa.a: Hafsa could have looked at the numbers for a few minutes each week with someone supportive, so a slow slide would show up while there were still several options.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini to watch a desk neighbour avoid the numbers?
qa.a: Nandini feels uneasy and unsure, wanting to say more but not wanting to push, so the joke was as far as it went.

grounding: The account shows a founder skipping the dashboard weekly until the bank forces a look, by which time the decline is long and choices are fewer.

Monday, 2 June. Rashmi's weekly dashboard email arrives: "Your numbers this week". Rashmi archives it unopened. "Next week, when things pick up," she tells her co-founder, Jyoti, who raises an eyebrow.
Monday, 4 August. Another email, another archive. Jyoti asks at stand-up, "How are renewals looking?" Rashmi says, "Fine, I think. I'll check." She doesn't. Just thinking about opening it makes her stomach drop.
Friday, 3 October. The bank sends a low-balance alert. Rashmi finally opens the dashboard and scrolls back. Renewals have fallen every week since June, four months straight. Jyoti reads over her shoulder, silent. In June they could have cut costs or tested a cheaper plan. Now there are seven weeks of cash and very few options left.

qa.q: What did the bank send on 3 October?
Why did Rashmi keep archiving the dashboard email?
qa.a: Just thinking about it made her stomach drop; she was anxious about bad news and kept hoping things would pick up.

qa.q: What could Rashmi have done in June?
qa.a: Opened the dashboard every week, even when it was painful, and shared it with Jyoti so they could cut costs or test a cheaper plan early.

qa.q: How does Jyoti experience the October discovery?
qa.a: Jyoti is silent and likely shaken, realising her questions were brushed aside while the options disappeared.

grounding: It shows a founder avoiding a painful dashboard for months until a bank alert forces a look, by which time four months of decline have narrowed the options.

passage:
Anjali Masi poured the tea and watched Bidisha push her laptop away with a sigh. "Don't do what I did. When I was twenty-four I ran a small online saree business. Every Monday the sales report came in, and every Monday I didn't open it. I told myself I was busy. Really, I was afraid of what it would say.
Four months went like that. Then one day the bank called: the account couldn't cover the weavers' payment. That night I finally read all the reports. Sales had been sliding since the very first week I stopped looking. If I'd seen it in the first month, I could have changed my prices, cut the photoshoots or called my best customers. By then I could only close the website and pay the weavers what I owed, slowly.
So open your numbers, Bidisha. Especially when you don't want to."

qa.a: The bank called because the account couldn't cover the weavers' payment.

qa.q: Why did young Anjali not open the Monday sales report?
qa.a: She was afraid of what it would say, and told herself she was busy to avoid that fear.

qa.q: Which choice in the story could have changed the outcome, and why?
qa.a: Reading the report in the first month, because she could still have changed prices, cut photoshoots or called her best customers.

qa.q: How might the weavers have been affected?
qa.a: The weavers were paid late and slowly, which likely strained their trust and their own household budgets.

grounding: It shows a young founder skipping weekly sales reports out of fear until a bank call forces a look, revealing four months of decline and few options left.
